title: Chaliapin becomes the prophet
question: How does Chaliapin build from the traveller’s quiet story to God’s final command in these two performances?
intro: A traveller meets a six-winged seraph in the desert; the angel tears out his heart and puts a burning coal in its place. Rimsky-Korsakov gives Pushkin’s terrible vision to a bass voice, beginning quietly and ending with God’s command to speak. Chaliapin recorded it with Percy Pitt in 1921 and returned to it with Albert Coates in 1927.

recordings.label: Fyodor Chaliapin, Percy Pitt
recordings.note: Bass and orchestra recorded through an acoustic horn at Hayes, during Chaliapin’s first English visit since before the war.

recordings.label: Fyodor Chaliapin, Albert Coates
recordings.note: The microphone remake, recorded at London’s Small Queen’s Hall on 20 October 1927, with Coates conducting the orchestra.

passages.label: The traveller speaks
passages.note: The bass tells his story in measured phrases. Flowing notes in the accompaniment surround the voice as the seraph appears.

passages.label: The voice rises
passages.note: The bass reaches higher over rippling accompaniment, describing the sounds that fill the traveller’s newly opened ears.

passages.label: A pause in the telling
passages.note: The accompaniment continues between the sung phrases, growing softer and slowing before the story resumes.

passages.label: God’s command
passages.note: The bass delivers God’s charge above firm chords. Rimsky-Korsakov marks the passage con forza e maestoso: forcefully and majestically.
